prose: Hardly could I remember when and how my passion for reading took place. Nevertheless, since I started gaining awareness of the surroundings, my memory has revolved around colorful wrapped books that my brother received every passing birthday. Unlike the oldest sibling who was brought up with strict rules and expectations, I often found my parents’ “easiness" on me as both a blessing and a curse. Being raised in a culture where educational investment is still in favor of boys, I have been struggling to seek recognition from the adults, which is via defining my own identity, more than just a craving for attention. Such a desire has fueled and been fueled by the fondness for reading from early stages of life, further transforming into my pride with writing upon the present.

As a quiet yet impulsive kid, I often found it hard to articulate my own thoughts into words. I secretly established mixed feelings of admiration and jealousy towards my brother, whose cheerful, fun-loving personality along with humorous communication style managed to brighten various social gatherings, thus flattering our mother most of the time. Although I was relieved by the fact that my parents rarely criticized nor stressed me out about school work, it was quite obvious to me that the name they mentioned to our relatives had always been my brother’s. Without proper guidance, I became terribly reserved and rebellious. Since I refused to speak, the teachers grew tired of my unpredictably adverse manners. Until we were all aware of the issue, there was already a huge bridge in communication that prevented my parents from understanding and helping their introverted and stubborn daughter out. They had no choice but to let me skip 3 years of kindergarten, which is the crucial window for socializing in general and exposure to school life in particular. As concepts and significance of learning were too vague for me to understand, I jumped to the conclusion that I was simply incapable of academic performance for the half part of my childhood.

Referring back to my older brother, I found myself under his shadows not only in terms of social attention but also my unconscious tendency of imitation. In respect to that, I admitted the 1 year age gap had facilitated his influence on almost all my hobbies, tastes, and interests.

Since my family had always known that my brother was fond of reading, it was not unusual for them to give him a stack of books for birthdays ever since he turned 7; likewise, it was not usual for me to share the gifts after him. At first, both my parents and I only assumed that as a passive mirroring act. Indeed, such a decoding process of written communication has provoked my curiosity about the world and nurtured the yearning for knowledge. From the simple storytelling of plots and characters’ traits, in which materials from various corners of life were encapsulated, the books put my vague understanding of people and events together. There is no exaggeration to say that they were the first channels to connect my awareness with the surroundings.

Feeling at ease in reading, I then proceeded with Vietnamese literature textbooks that were included in my mandatory curriculum. I started asking my parents about the words’ definitions within these texts just to keep up with the stories’ flows and their general indications, which pleasantly surprised them since I had never questioned (or had found no motives to question) about school tasks before. With their support, I made progress in completing all the comprehension assignments without skipping any pieces of poems, short prose, and dialogues. I even advanced greatly as to proceed with texts within my brothers’ grade and higher, ones that he barely started whereas I had finished reading from the preceding summers before school started. The more readings that I moved forward with, the broader scope of vocabulary that I acquired. My parents also felt no hesitation to purchase a thick Vietnamese dictionary so that I could look up unknown words on my own in case they were not available to help. It should be noted that reading books did not instantly spark my interest in learning, nor did it directly fuel any moment of realization. It was the ongoing thoughts that “I finally understand things”/ “I am now aware of what is happening” that slowly cleared the inferiority complex and self-doubt about my cognitive ability.

It was not long before my devotion with writing followed. On the mid-autumn festival of my second grade, our grandparents, who lived far away, sent my brother and me those charming holiday gifts. As we both felt an urge to write them thank you notes in return, my little letter to grandma did take my family aback. Are you thinking that my writing was so proficient that they were delighted by the newly-discovered talent? Indeed, they were shocked by my comparison between the Carp Lantern that I received and our beloved grandma’s facial features. Although I had to rewrite it so that her heart won’t accidentally hurt, my parents did compliment me on my ability to use “imaginative” simile and fluent expression since it was the very first time that I had ever composed a letter. This however encouraged me to try and practice different types of writing later on.

Thankfully, my enjoyment of reading books synchronized well with that of writing essays, as much as how my receptive and expressive channels both circulated to appreciate the beauty of written language. Whether it was a noteworthy piece of fiction or a lighthearted slice of manga, I always found it helpful to learn from their unique author’s voice or integrated systems of ideas. Not until I attended middle school did my writing ability blossomed to the fullest. Those were also the years when I was most passionate in reading and began picking up more challenging literature. I skipped my daily nap time that I usually loved, spent all my summer indoors instead of going to the pool, and heading to the local bookstore on my own instead of karaoke boxes after school like the other kids just to immerse myself in the cognitive world with books. “Nobody’s boy”, “The Call of the Wild”, or “The Notre-Dame Cathedral” were some of the earliest entries that prompted my navigation through the world’s classics.

Reading has sharpened my pen to a greater extent, especially the ability to use words flexibly. It became more frequent for me to earn excellent grades for papers, but I knew my strength lay in the argumentative area where individual identity was held in high regard. Promotion in the writing career came to me smoothly after that; I participated in the Literature team, endured extra-hour training, and competed with other schools in the region. However, one of the most glorious achievements throughout my lifetime has always been my admission in VNU-HCM High School for Gifted, the top 1 institute in my nation, with only 35 available seats out of nearly 700 candidates in the application pool for the Literature Specialized Class.

As I was at the peak that qualified me as “capable of writing” in the first year of high school, I was also at a trough for losing touch with my literate identity. With perfect choices of words, my talent in utilizing, organizing, and displaying languages makes any piece of writing pleasantly aesthetic and emotional to the readers. However, I was incapable of sensing any emotions at all, even questioning myself as being hypocritical. I lacked the true inspiration, or the breakthrough of ideas that I could take pride of. There was neither any creativity nor exploration, just the well-composed but empty demonstration of words. Like a robot, I could process fluent writing without thinking much of what really motivated me from the inside. It seemed as if I had possessed a skill, but not the spirit of a true writer. I have always hated the word "skill", as it sounds so rigid, modeled, and alienated from the concept of composition or the whole creative world that my heart belongs to. Full of shame and disappointment, writing was no longer something I would gladly seek pleasure in, but rather a burden that even hindered me from holding the pen. Words are not just tools to compose a successful work; sadly, I was the one who led them to become that way.

Taking a break from writing, I decided to pick up reading again after many years occupied with a stressful life, which I can never appreciate enough up until now. The more I read, the more I realized how cramped and narrow my literacy world was. Reading has blown to my lost soul a breath of fresh air, filling my vain mind with the generosity of language. After years of studying abroad, exposure to a new culture, language, and tons of ups and downs, my perspectives have been freshly enriched over and over. At present, I focus writing about the internal transformation as well as personal growth more than the unreal experience to which I do not relate. Perhaps my world has not been broad enough to extend my potential beyond the highest level of Maslow’s Hierarchy of needs; still, I am trying my best every day to reach fulfillment in the self-actualization stage. I am strongly aware that there is still plenty of room for improvement, to the same extent of how critical my mission is in adjusting my writing ego before I attempt to sympathize with others.

I used to be at a loss until finding my own place with reading and writing. Not only have they guided me through the world that is full of prejudice and blind spots, but they also helped me stare into my own heart that is filled with flaws. After years of commitment, I find my role as a reader and writer has become increasingly challenging yet satisfying. I am not planning to pursue the corresponding professional path, and it is not because realism has pushed such a childhood dream out of reach. It just happens to me that we do not need to make money from our passion. If one day I felt compelled to put down words in exchange of materialistic values, or being dishonest with my own ideals and values ever again, I would hate myself as well as writing for the rest of my life.
“Look at you, you resemble Dracula as to keep wearing All-Black”

Never before had I paid attention to such a concern. Given that the influence of villains in general tend to exceed most of my favorite movies’ protagonists, and the fact that Black links strongly with my inherited traits of hair and eyes, my preference for this particular color has gone beyond ordinary sense. Whether going to school or taking a walk around the neighborhood, I have always chosen Black as my top fashion choice. Putting on a solid black jacket most of the time has left people with an impression of a tough person who would never be disturbed by spare emotions.

My distant appearance sets a parallel effect towards my disposition, at least in the way others perceive about me: a kid who passed her puberty peacefully, enjoys doing origami as a pastime, and would rather listen to folk instrumental music than cheesy love songs or heavy raps. Little do they know these without-lyrics-melodies are preferred so that my innermost feelings would not be interpreted. Nor do they understand those repeated folds I had on the paper cranes were one of the methods I used to suppress the impulsive aggression which has always been part of my nature. It is also no wonder that applying for a Literature major in the home country’s high school took my parents by surprise. I spent my day and night in middle school solving statistical problems, then declaring the opposing major at the final moment in an attempt to rationalize tons of my inner concerns.

Facilitated by these disguised impressions, the psychological effect of wearing Black curiously helps me feel more secure and make sure personal weaknesses are not exposed in front of others. Unconsciously immersed in my model as a rational creature, I have always prided myself on keeping my manners and mental state in check. The most dangerous part was that, even myself was tricked into believing that way, and started embracing that role-playing so intensively that I tend to lose my own identity. I convinced myself that emotions are the most useless thing of human-beings and that it was critical to get rid of them. The situation became worse and worse when I ignored my friends’ negative concerns, avoided all kinds of social communication, and isolated myself from the dramatic school life. I deactivated any emotional-related thoughts and imprisoned my rebellious, sensitive nature inside the Black jacket.

It is not alien to the boarding students that I put on my typical black outfit, silently sitting among them on a weekend shuttle to Target. But only I know wearing black that day represents something else, which is a signal of grief. For the very first time, I wished someone had come and questioned my usual somber fashion sense, so that I would naturally burst into tears: “My grandpa, he’s gone.” What disappointed me was not because people failed to recognize my sadness the moment I needed their attention and sympathy; frankly, there was no point for them to do what I expected. But the most apathetic part was that I myself was incapable of the most basic mourning.

It turned out that I had been forcing myself into adopting such a standoffish model for so long that my capacity for facial expression was decayed. Ironically, the Black color that I had been using in order to handle the fragile emotions then served as an only emotional transmitter. Other than compensating for my deficiency in expression function, Black from this traumatic experience has supplemented an aspect of realization towards introspection: it was a foolish attempt to confide myself in any stereotypes. It reminds how foolish I was to obsess over a group identity that I lose my own as a fully functioning person.

The following days, black clothes have continued to act as my defense mechanism during social interactions. However, via the same outfit choices, my friends have found me striking conversations with multiple-word sentences, laughing more after a joke, and displaying sympathy towards a teammate’s illness. Accepting the existence of minor flaws or turbulent emotions, I become more tolerant towards myself and let my inconsistent nature be compatible with any challenges. My lifelong goal has revolved around keeping these special shades on track, to the extent of how I honor the power of being well-balanced. Just like the way the color Black can both guard and give out signals, I try to adjust my manners and emotional state in the way that my identity is appreciated.
I believe that the opposite of life is not death, but to exist without feeling alive.

Detachment takes many forms to withdraw such a privilege from us, and imprisonment is perhaps the most conceivable yet cruelest misfortune that God imposed on every man. It is because the concept does not simply indicate being confined behind bars that once we break them, we gain real freedom. In two famous works The Allegory of the Cave and The House of Asterion, Plato and Jorge Luis Borges, respectively, managed to discuss the mutual theme of imprisonment in a way that complemented their own belief via creative choices, effects, and moral solutions.

First of all, imprisonment within the two texts both revolves around the effect on mentality. In The House of Asterion, the protagonist was trapped inside a labyrinth alone due to his special background. Although he claimed to have a certain form of freedom, what actually imprisons him is his mentality and constant state of isolation. As for the Allegory of the Cave, the concept of imprisonment is more obvious and well-defined. The dialogue between two philosophers discusses the scenario in which a group of prisoners were locked up in a cave since birth. Not only were they lost their freedom to the visible setting but also had their knowledge confined to the reflected images from the shadow they saw in that cave. Indeed, the given physical conditions throughout the two storylines play a common role in implying multiple forms of mental imprisonment that their characters had undergone. The dark, vast, and empty setup from the minotaur’s labyrinth and the prisoners’ cave are both utilized to deprive their occupants, whether voluntarily or obligatorily, of the most basic cognitive abilities.
Metaphorically, those created a misleading effect as to make the victims preoccupied with themselves and their own illusional worldviews.

Despite sharing the intention of how external settings imply one’s inner mental prison, Plato and Jorge conduct their own interpretation of the theme, which can be seen in the particular choices of literacy techniques and thereby different effects on readers. While The House of Asterion was composed in the short story genre that best suits the narration of a mythology figure, Plato’s use of highly theoretical dialogue corresponds to his tone and role as a philosopher. The explicit display of speeches via such a written communication device engages readers in discussing the topics at a faster pace with little effort to understand the theme as a whole, since there is no need to gather separate elements across the reading. Imprisonment itself is a vague concept; therefore, comments and insight continuously provided and updated by the experts are especially helpful to uplift our understanding of the theme. In the other words, the dialogue used in The Allegory of the Cave manages to blend such a complicated philosophical question in pleasantly digestible reading. In this respect, Plato brings our attention to an unlikely scenario, which is the imprisonment from birth of a group of people who perceive things via shadows for their entire life. Creating scenarios prompted and fueled readers’ imagination. More importantly, it allows the writer to manipulate and rationalize the theme freely in the manner that best communicates his own belief. On the other hand, allowing readers to progressively explore the truth upon collecting and connecting pieces of details without going off-topic thanks to the focused, well-structured plot and cast make the short story an effective delivery for the House of Asterion. This is hard to do in novels and movies whose massive length might distract us from appreciating the theme in its complete sense. However short, the creative development of plot in the House of Asterion still keeps its ideas from full disclosure thus requiring readers to contemplate the morals in different angles and depth. This interestingly parallels the personal theme of the story, where our discovery of the plot resembles the character’s attempt to navigate his labyrinth. Mental imprisonment in this scenario cannot be broken via escapism, but rather by freeing ourselves from blind assumptions and appreciating life in various perspectives.

The two texts’ different aspects of focus also demonstrate their unique moral direction of the theme. Although they both aim to foreshadow the mental form of imprisonment, it appears that The House of Asterion concentrates more on an outcast’s social withdrawal whereas The Allegory of the Cave mainly discusses unenlightenment of a disadvantaged group. Unlike those in the latter story who lost their freedom to some sort of laws, Asterion actually did have a chance to leave his labyrinth and reach out to the exterior world. However, his identity was not acknowledged by the common people, leading the minotaur to “return to solitude”, isolate himself, and embrace self-absorption. The character became the prisoner of his own mind who lost the ability to appreciate the world beyond personal lens. Since redemption cannot be found anywhere in reality where every of his presence was rejected by society and where his soul was already filled with sins, the kind of freedom that Asterion was desperate and craving for the most is through death, which is regarded as ultimate self-transformation rather than the end of one’s life. Contrastingly, the people in The Allegory of the Cave had completely lost control of their own fate since birth. Their delusional perception was a result of limited access to the outside world. Therefore, these people still had a choice to obtain “freedom” beyonds the cave to fill their eyes and soul with the lightness of knowledge. We can see that in an attempt to free themselves from mental imprisonment, which has something to do with self-absorption and cognitive bias in both cases, self-transcendence is a key solution. However, Asterion got rid of himself by the redemption through death while the prisoners decided whether or not to step out of the darkness and seek enlightenment from an unexplored world.

In summary, other than similarly utilizing physical settings to discuss underlying mental imprisonment, the creative choices and aspects of focus in the two texts lead Plato and Jorge to implement their unique directions for the theme. They point out that imprisonment can take many forms, which in these scenarios when people are confined, isolated, and lost in their own illusions of the surrounding world. Depending on each context, one might either await redemption via death or gain enlightenment by knowledge. Regardless of the moral solutions, we can learn from the above literacy works that self-transcendence, the rising above oneself, is the yearning desire for which those victims of mental imprisonment have been seeking for th most part of their life.

prose: Almost a century has passed since World War II; still, its echoes persist as unhealed trauma thanks to the practice of literacy and visual works. Unlike the horror genre, antiwar stories “haunt” people without the use of jump scare, or constant fear, but via the heightened emotions and lasting sorrow shared among protagonists and viewers that altogether develop an aversion to war. According to Cato Conroy (2017), an antiwar film “is any movie that makes war look horrible” by “highlighting the futility of it all, the psychological impact, or even the impact on a family” (Conroy, para.#2,13). In evaluating titles that have been capable of transmitting such a humanitarian mission, the Japanese animation Grave of the Fireflies surprisingly turns out to be one of the most outstanding candidates. Despite socio-political subjectiveness, the 90-minute movie manages to depict the destructiveness of war due to great investment in setting, symbolism, and character depth.

Grave of the Fireflies is a Japanese tragedy anime about two young siblings’ struggle for survival during World War II. After escaping from the firebombed house, Seita (brother) and Setsuko (sister) are adopted by Aunt Yokokawa, a distant relative of their deceased mother. Life is not easy under the same roof where the children continuously receive offenses from the selfish aunt, which later causes them to move away to live on their own in an abandoned bomb shelter. As time flies, the excessive lack of nutrition and proper hygiene makes the siblings suffer greatly, and Seita does not miss a chance to feed his little sister, even resorting to stealing crops and is beaten severely later on. Tragically, when Seita finally manages to bring food home, little Setsuko has gone forever while her brother is attempting to cook their first hearty meal.

The movie is based on the true story of Akiyuki Nosaka who wrote the novel of the same name as expressing regret and grief towards his lost sister during World War II. Since it was reenacted in 1988 by the director and founder of Studio Ghibli, Takahata Isao, the film immediately received tons of compliments and has been recorded to move many audiences to tears with a 100% score on Rotten Tomatoes (Grave of the Fireflies, n.d). According to New York Times’ top critic Glenn Kenny (2019), it is “One of the most startling and moving animated films ever” (Kenny, para.#4). Heartbreaking and powerful, Grave of the Fireflies is undoubtedly a successful film work in the sense that generates contemplation of humanity beyond basic emotional touch.

Despite being an animated movie, Grave of the Fireflies does a great job in portraying honestly the brutality of war setting. The film illustrates a devastated Kobe, Japan’s port city, during World War II. Familiar associations of the war, whether visual or auditorial, are utilized effectively and contribute to most graphic scenes - from the repeated appearance of US combat aircraft and rapid firebombs to scarce resources of food, shabby bomb shelters, and charred bodies of unfortunates. One of the most impressive scenes is as people flee from emerging bomb attacks, wooden houses burst into flames and successively collapse into the roads, crushing down the entire town but the riverside along with ill-fated innocents. Emphasizing still poses and focusing less on motions, Takahata’s drawing style of landscapes and design choice of characters successfully adds realism to the movie. Thanks to the sophisticated artwork and proficient sound effects, these setting elements altogether lead audiences to the tough, desperate wartime even though we have never really been there ourselves.

It is not only the external contexts that display the destructiveness of war, but the complexity of the characters also gives audiences valuable insight into this theme. In the movie, Seita appears to be a young 14-year-old boy who has to take on tons of responsibilities in the absence of his parents. While the character’s genuine love and care for his sister Setsuko are unquestionable, Seita is not built as a flawless figure. War is harsh in terms that it forces people to grapple with dilemmas, and the protagonist himself as a teenager is not mature enough to avoid making mistakes. Impulsive and full of pride, Seita’s decision to leave the aunt’s house indirectly leads to the siblings’ suffering and Setsuko’s death afterward. Despite the farmer’s advice, he refuses to return and apologize to his aunt even when Setsuko is enduring serious malnourishment symptoms. This is also said to be the biggest regret of Akiyuki Nosaka, the original author of the story, as he rewrites his experience in Seita’s name. Furthermore, the character’s illegal commitment when he attempts to steal crops from the neighbor, also reveals the negative effect of war on human nature. Extreme hunger and poverty take away moral standards from a previously well-educated boy, making him resort to wrongful methods to get by. This aspect of the war on human characteristics is also showcased by Aunt Yokokawa. The aunt plays her role as a selfish and strict guardian of the siblings after their mother’s death. Although she first appears to feel sorry and care greatly for her niece and nephew, Aunt Yokokawa refuses to feed the children enough rice during meals and frequently insults them for being such a burden. This however is not a sudden shift in the character’s personalities. Instead, her tough attitudes toward Setsuko and Seita is a proof of the war's cruel consequences. Those days of upheaval make everything luxurious, and to survive on one’s own is hard, let alone to feed three mouths. Therefore, it is evident that adversity turns the aunt into a tough and narrow-hearted woman, even with her family members. Adding depth to these characters by having their personalities and backgrounds distorted, the movie manages to point out the brutality of war with a humanistic approach.

From the title itself, Grave of Fireflies’ use of symbolism contributes to the overall theme of war’s brutality. Throughout the movie, fireflies take multiple forms that contain significant metaphorical meanings, one of which is the idea of fragility (Medzińska, 2020). In the dark shelter where the siblings live, fireflies serve as their sole lighting resource, and possibly implied further as a beam of hope in the darkest phases of life. However, such a natural beauty does not last long until the following morning, when Setsuko buries the dead fireflies in a grave and questions these insects' and their mother’s loss. Sadly, this is also a signal of the little girl’s short fate eventually, as they all represent the ups and downs of life. The fireflies also resemble firebombs as they are simultaneously shot from warplanes. In this scenario, their flaring lights however symbolize destructiveness. Having these two representatives blended in the movie poster, where Setsuko and Seita stand under a sky full of fireflies, the film suggests that the siblings’ hope for survival is fragile in the theme of crisis. Their contrasting meanings surprisingly complement each other and ultimately highlight the aversive war theme.

The only factor that makes the movie controversial to global audiences is its socio-political context. As the idea of nationalism is somewhat accentuated, it incidentally gives a bias that prefers the Japanese as the sole victims and the US army as leading to the tragedy. Subjectiveness in the assumed roles distracts audiences from appreciating the movie in the complete sense of war criticism. Fortunately, the effect of this particular aspect is discernible, given that the movie gains greater focus on the emotional development of the plot and characters and less on combats.

In summary, the setting, characters, and symbolism reflect the destructiveness of war in various aspects, whereas the subjectiveness in the socio-political context slightly distracts the theme. The movie draws out many consequences that war leaves by depicting the significance of loss as well as the decline of humanity. This includes having many realistic war associations in the illustration, which helps the audiences better relate to the protagonists’ backgrounds. Moreover, the film’s focus on the characters’ depth and use of metaphors make it more internally valuable. Since people’s emotional experiences are greatly satisfied by these elements, their concern for political bias is minor. Beautifully tragic and profoundly ethical, Grave of Fireflies is an unmissable masterpiece that goes beyond the animation market.
